questions.sub_skill: Detect misconfigurations and runtime risks in container workloads by using Defender for Containers
questions.prompt: Why is binary drift a stronger signal inside a container than the equivalent would be on a virtual machine?
options: Containers write far fewer files, so any write is anomalous

A container is supposed to be exactly its image and nothing else, so a process that did not come from the image is close to definitional evidence of compromise; on a VM, administrators legitimately install things
The Defender sensor cannot see process activity on VMs
Containers cannot be patched in place, so binaries never change legitimately
questions.explanation: The detection works because the platform's constraints are tighter. Drift detection alerts on unauthorised external processes running inside a container; drift blocking stops them, and the two are separate settings.
why_not: The strength of the signal is not about write volume. A container should be exactly its image, so any process that did not come from it is suspect.
Defender does see process activity on VMs. The point is that on a VM, installing things is normal.
Binaries can be changed inside a running container - that is exactly what drift detection catches. The argument is that doing so is never the legitimate path, whereas on a VM it often is.

questions.sub_skill: Detect misconfigurations and runtime risks in container workloads by using Defender for Containers
questions.prompt: Defender for Containers reports no vulnerabilities for a running workload, and the registry shows its source image as clean. Why might the running container still be vulnerable?
options: Registry scanning covers images at rest; assessing running images additionally requires agentless machine scanning plus either K8s API access or the Defender sensor
The image may have been pulled from a registry you do not scan
Language-package vulnerabilities are never reported, only OS packages
Running containers are assessed only once, at admission
questions.explanation: Two things are true. The prerequisites for assessing running images differ from those for registry images, and a cluster can pull from anywhere — a clean registry does not mean a clean cluster. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management covers OS and language packages.
why_not: Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management covers language packages as well as OS packages.
Assessing running images is not an admission-time check. It depends on the prerequisites above, and on the image's registry being scanned at all.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
questions.prompt: A cluster has Microsoft Entra integration and Kubernetes RBAC enabled. An engineer who left the company last month still runs kubectl successfully. Give the two most likely explanations.
options: Local accounts are still enabled, so the --admin path works and is not auditable
Permissions were defined in cluster manifests rather than as Azure role assignments, so they did not disappear when the account left the directory
The cluster's API server has no authorised IP ranges
The kubelet identity retains AcrPull
questions.explanation: Local accounts are enabled by default and --admin remains a non-auditable backdoor even with Entra integration and RBAC. Separately, Kubernetes RBAC bindings live in the cluster and outlive the employee; Azure RBAC for Kubernetes puts them under Entra. Note that disabling local accounts on an existing cluster also requires rotating the cluster certificates.
why_not: Authorised IP ranges restrict where the API server can be reached from. They do not explain why the engineer's credential still works.
AcrPull on the kubelet identity lets nodes pull images. It gives an engineer no kubectl access.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls for Azure Container Registry
questions.prompt: A pipeline authenticates to Azure Container Registry with the admin account. What is wrong, and what replaces it?
options: Nothing — the admin account is the supported automation path
It is a single shared credential with push rights and no identity behind it; disable it and use Entra with AcrPush for the pipeline and AcrPull on the cluster's kubelet identity
It is fine for pipelines but must be disabled for clusters
It should be replaced with an anonymous pull token
questions.explanation: The admin account is the storage account key problem from 02-01 in a different costume. Entra authentication with AcrPull and AcrPush role assignments removes the shared credential, and attaching the registry to AKS grants AcrPull to the kubelet identity so no registry credential exists anywhere.
why_not: The admin account is a single shared credential with push rights and no identity behind it - the storage account key problem again.
It is no better for pipelines. Every holder shares one credential with push rights and no identity.
Anonymous pull removes authentication altogether. The goal is an identity behind every caller.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
questions.prompt: You want to guarantee that no privileged container can ever be created in a cluster, regardless of what a developer submits. Describe the mechanism.
options: A network policy denying pod-to-pod traffic
The Azure Policy for Kubernetes add-on, evaluating every request to the API server at admission before it is persisted, with the effect set to deny rather than audit
The Defender sensor, blocking the container at runtime
An admission webhook configured in the container registry
questions.explanation: Admission control is the only place to stop a privileged pod being created at all. With the add-on installed, every API server request is evaluated against your policies before it is persisted — and the audit-versus-deny choice is what decides whether you report or prevent.
why_not: A network policy controls pod-to-pod traffic. It does not stop a privileged pod being created.
The sensor detects at runtime, after the pod exists. Admission control is the only place to stop creation.
Admission control happens at the cluster's API server, not in the container registry.

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security controls for Azure Container Instances and Azure Container Apps
questions.prompt: A container app must pull from your registry and reach a key vault, with no credential stored anywhere, and must not be reachable from the internet. Which configuration?
options: External ingress with an IP allow-list, and a registry username and password in app settings
Internal ingress, a managed identity used for both the registry pull and the key vault, and secrets referenced from Key Vault rather than set as environment variables
External ingress with client certificate authentication, and the ACR admin account
Internal ingress and the ACR admin account, since the app is not public
questions.explanation: Internal ingress removes public reachability; the managed identity removes the registry credential and the key vault credential. Secrets in environment variables in the deployment definition are readable by anyone who can read the definition.
why_not: External ingress keeps the app on the internet, and a registry password in app settings is a stored credential.
External ingress is still internet-reachable, and the ACR admin account is a shared credential.
Internal ingress is right, but the ACR admin account is still a stored, shared credential.
